subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Power is the rate of doing work: P = dW/dt = F·v.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W): 1 W = 1 J/s.
For constant force and velocity: P = Fv cos θ (dot product).

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Mechanical energy (K + U) is conserved ONLY when all forces are conservative.
Friction and air resistance are non-conservative — they convert mechanical energy to heat.
The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) holds for ALL forces, conservative or not.
Total energy (including thermal) is always conserved — this is the first law of thermodynamics.
Choose the reference level for PE at the lowest point to simplify calculations.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Mechanical energy conservation: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f (only conservative forces)
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²
Work by non-conservative forces: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i)
Gravitational PE: U_g = mgh (near Earth); U = −GMm/r (universal)
Elastic PE: U_s = ½kx²; total spring energy: ½mv² + ½kx² = ½kA²

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: The law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed.
Mechanical energy (K + U) is conserved when only conservative forces do work.
The work-energy theorem states that the net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Mechanical energy conservation (K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f) is the most common problem type.
Work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) is more general — use it when friction is present.
Pendulum and spring problems are standard — know the energy oscillation formulas.
Smooth surface shortcut: mgh = ½mv² — mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) independent of mass.
Spring shortcut: ½kA² = ½mv² — max speed v = A√(k/m).

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Conservative forces (gravity, spring, electrostatic) allow potential energy definition.
Non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance) dissipate energy as heat.
The closed-loop test: if net work around a closed path is zero, the force is conservative.
When both types act, use W_nc = ΔE_mech (general energy equation).
Friction always does negative work — it removes mechanical energy from the system.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Conservative force: work depends only on endpoints; ∮F·dr = 0 (closed loop)
Non-conservative force: work depends on path; ∮F·dr ≠ 0
Work-energy relation: W_nc = ΔE_mech = (K_f + U_f) − (K_i + U_i)
Conservative force and PE: W = −ΔU (work = negative change in potential energy)
Friction work: W_f = −μNd (always negative; energy dissipated as heat)

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: A force is conservative if the work done depends only on initial and final positions, not the path.
The work done by a conservative force around any closed loop is zero: ∮F·dr = 0.
Non-conservative forces dissipate mechanical energy as heat, sound, or deformation.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: The closed-loop test is the standard way to justify whether a force is conservative.
Gravity, spring, and electrostatic forces are always conservative — memorize these.
Friction and air resistance are always non-conservative — they dissipate energy.
Closed-loop test: if net work around a closed path is zero, the force is conservative.
Path-independence shortcut: gravity, spring, and electrostatic forces are always conservative.
